before.diving: A highly specialized cold-water destination where drysuit-certified divers and snorkelers explore submerged icebergs and Arctic marine life, with only a very limited operator base. Most trips operate in the short summer window around Disko Bay or East Greenland.
before.birding: White-tailed Eagles soar over icy fjords, while the tundra holds breeding Gyrfalcons, Rock Ptarmigans and Snow Buntings. Boat trips to sea cliffs offer views of nesting Thick-billed Murres and millions of Little Auks. Greenland's birding focuses on Arctic specialists and massive seabird colonies rather than high species counts.
before.hotSprings: Uunartoq's hot spring, on an uninhabited island in South Greenland, has been used since Norse settlers arrived roughly 1,000 years ago — heated geothermally rather than volcanically, and warm year-round. The only way to actually reach it is an organized boat tour, which runs June through September; outside that window it's effectively cut off.
before.auroraChasing: Greenland's near-total lack of light pollution makes for some of the cleanest dark skies for aurora viewing anywhere, across a season that runs from late summer into spring.
before.whaleWatching: **Humpback** and **minke whales** feed among the icebergs of Disko Bay and the Nuuk fjords during the short Arctic summer, and **fin whales** are seen in Disko Bay and more often in South Greenland. Boat trips run primarily from June to September, offering close encounters with whales feeding in the nutrient-rich glacial meltwaters.
before.mountaineering: The Ilulissat and Disko Bay area is a boat-and-hiking destination rather than a climbing one. Greenland’s real climbing — the 1,000m-plus granite walls of Tasermiut Fjord in the far south, and expeditions in the east — is a separate, self-sufficient expedition by boat, with no mountain rescue and a season of roughly June to August.
before.wildlifeViewing: Muskoxen and reindeer are frequently seen on tundra safaris around Kangerlussuaq, Greenland's most reliable land-based wildlife viewing. In the coastal fjords, ringed and harp seals are common year-round. Polar bears are occasionally spotted on late-summer expedition cruises into East Greenland's Scoresby Sund, but are rarely encountered on standard west coast itineraries. Arctic foxes are occasionally spotted scavenging near settlements.

before.safari: Beyond highland specialties like **gelada baboons** and the **Ethiopian wolf**, Ethiopia offers some traditional safari game viewing. Awash National Park holds **beisa oryx**, **Soemmerring's gazelle**, **greater kudu** and **hamadryas baboons**, while Nechisar National Park, grassland between Lakes Abaya and Chamo, has **Burchell's zebra** and **hippo** and **crocodile** boat trips. Omo and Mago in the far south hold elusive **elephants** and **buffalo**.
before.birding: More than 850 bird species, including around 30 regional highland endemics like the Thick-billed Raven and striking Blue-winged Goose. Wattled Ibis and Black-winged Lovebird are found in the highlands near Addis Ababa, and in the Bale Mountains Rouget's Rails are commonly seen in the alpine moorlands. The localized Prince Ruspoli's Turaco is reliably found in southern juniper woodlands, while the arid south holds the highly restricted Stresemann's Bushcrow.
before.mountaineering: Ethiopia has no real mountaineering scene: Ras Dashen, the highest peak (about 4,550m), is a trek rather than a climb, and Tullu Deemtu in the Bale Mountains can be reached by road. The one genuine climbing draw is the red sandstone towers of Gheralta, with crack and tower climbing on variable rock and only a handful of documented routes.
before.wildlifeViewing: Gelada baboon troops are virtually guaranteed in the Simien Mountains, often grazing in groups of hundreds alongside the Walia ibex, found exclusively on the steep escarpments there. The endangered Ethiopian wolf, one of Africa's rarest mammals, is most reliably spotted on the Sanetti Plateau in the Bale Mountains. Viewing requires high-altitude trekking or 4x4 access, with success heavily dependent on dry trail conditions.
before.wildflowerBlooms: The Meskel daisy (Adey Abeba) blankets highland fields yellow each September, timed to the end of the rainy season — but its fame is tied more to the Meskel festival itself (a UN-recognized cultural celebration, held September 27) than to flower-tourism in its own right. Worth knowing about if you're there for Meskel; not a reason to plan a trip around on its own.

before.diving: The Atlantic coast has real, modest diving — cooler water than the Mediterranean, a clear secondary activity to the souks and mountain trekking.
before.birding: Moussier's Redstart and Levaillant's Woodpecker draw birders to the scrub and forests of the High Atlas. The region offers excellent chances for North African specialties, including African Crimson-winged Finches and Tristram's Warblers in the higher elevations. Bearded Vultures are occasionally spotted soaring over the peaks of Toubkal National Park.
before.surfing: Taghazout, on the Atlantic coast near Agadir, is Morocco's surf capital — a real, well-established scene built around a long right-hand point break (Anchor Point) and a genuine year-round season, thanks to consistent Atlantic swell.
before.windSports: Essaouira, on Morocco's Atlantic coast, has earned the nickname "the Windy City of Africa" — the Alizée trade winds blow nearly all year, funneled and accelerated by the coastal terrain. April through October is the real season, peaking July through September; winter is calmer but rarely windless.
before.mountaineering: The Atlas offers three different draws: Taghia’s limestone walls, up to 800m and world-class multi-pitch climbing, a 5–6 hour 4x4 drive from Marrakech plus a walk-in; Todra Gorge’s roughly 400 routes far to the east; and Toubkal (4,167m), a winter crampons-and-axe ascent with ski touring in season. Rock seasons are April–May and September–October.
before.beachesSwimming: Beach swimming is a secondary feature here — Marrakech is inland, and the Atlantic coast (Essaouira-style) it borders runs cool and often windy rather than classic warm-Mediterranean, even in summer.
before.wildlifeViewing: Barbary macaques are frequently seen in lower valleys and near Ouzoud Falls, while elusive Barbary sheep (aoudad) navigate the steep slopes of Toubkal National Park. The arid foothills support rare Cuvier's gazelles, and high peaks host Golden Eagles and Bearded Vultures. Reptiles like the Mediterranean chameleon are present but require guided night walks to spot reliably.

before.safari: The Maasai Mara and Amboseli anchor Kenya's traditional vehicle safaris, built around big cats, massive **elephant** herds, and the Great Migration. From July to October, **wildebeest** and **zebra** pour into the Mara, facing **crocodiles** at river crossings, while Amboseli reliably delivers elephants walking beneath Mount Kilimanjaro. The long rains of April and May close many camps, making the dry seasons the clear time to go.
before.birding: Secretarybirds stride across the open plains of the Maasai Mara, hunting in the tall grass. These savanna reserves hold more than 500 bird species, featuring charismatic residents like the Kori Bustard, Southern Ground-Hornbill, and Lilac-breasted Roller. Vultures and eagles are abundant, often seen circling thermals, while Amboseli's wetlands draw large flocks of Lesser Flamingos and Gray Crowned-Cranes.
before.mountaineering: Neither the Maasai Mara nor Amboseli offers climbing — these are safari parks. The real objectives are separate trips: Mount Kenya (Batian, 5,199m, and Nelion, 5,188m, are technical rock; Point Lenana, 4,985m, is the trek) lies roughly 400km from Amboseli, and Hell’s Gate near Lake Naivasha has a small novice climbing tower about two hours from Nairobi.
before.wildlifeViewing: Lions, leopards, and cheetahs are reliably seen year-round across the Maasai Mara's open plains, while Amboseli guarantees massive herds of elephants against the backdrop of Mount Kilimanjaro. Resident populations of giraffes, zebras, hippos, and spotted hyenas are omnipresent across both reserves. Black rhinos are elusive but occasionally spotted in the Mara Triangle.

before.birding: High-altitude specialties like the Ibisbill and Himalayan Snowcock draw birders to the Tian Shan mountains. Summer trekking routes around Issyk-Kul and alpine passes offer chances to see White-browed Tit-Warblers, Bearded Vultures, and various redstarts.
before.hotSprings: Altyn Arashan ("Golden Spa"), a remote alpine valley near Karakol reached by jeep track or hike, is prized for water rich in radon and hydrogen sulfide — nearly every guesthouse in the small settlement has its own soaking pool. The access road and guesthouses only operate June through September; the rest of the year it's snowed in.
before.mountaineering: Central Asia’s big-range mountaineering — Lenin Peak (7,134m) is one of the least technical 7,000m peaks, and Khan Tengri (7,010m) is a serious objective reached by helicopter. The season runs late June to early September, Lenin Peak and Inylchek need a border-zone permit, and Ala-Archa near Bishkek offers more accessible alpine climbing.
before.wildlifeViewing: Kyrgyzstan’s Tian Shan mountains hold the elusive snow leopard and massive Argali (Marco Polo sheep), though both are genuinely rare and require dedicated, high-altitude expeditions to spot. General trekkers in summer alpine pastures frequently see long-tailed marmots and soaring Golden Eagles, while Siberian ibex are occasionally spotted on steep, rocky ridges with binoculars.
before.wildflowerBlooms: The high alpine meadows around Song-Köl and Jyrgalan fill with wildflowers once the passes open for summer, part of the same trekking season as the region's lakes and yurt stays rather than a standalone destination.

before.diving: Malaysian Borneo is a world-class destination for coral reef scenery, featuring deep main sites down to 130 ft. Sipadan is permit-limited and needs Advanced Open Water, with divers based at Mabul or Kapalai. Divers and snorkelers can expect guaranteed green turtles, along with likely sightings of barracuda schools and reef sharks. The best conditions run from March to October, avoiding the rougher seas of the northeast monsoon.
before.safari: River safaris on the Kinabatangan River are the core of a Borneo safari, offering dawn and dusk boat trips to see wild **orangutans**, **proboscis monkeys**, and occasionally **Bornean pygmy elephants**. Land-based viewing in Danum Valley and Tabin Wildlife Reserve adds chances for **banteng** and elusive **clouded leopards**. The dry season from May to September concentrates wildlife along the riverbanks for the most reliable sightings.
before.birding: Malaysian Borneo has over 680 bird species, about 60 endemic, led by the bizarre canopy-dwelling Bornean Bristlehead. Eight hornbill species are reliably seen from boats on the Kinabatangan River, and the endemic Whitehead's Trogon can be spotted in Mount Kinabalu's cloud forest. In Danum Valley, patient trekking can turn up elusive ground-dwellers like the Great Argus, Bornean Ground-Cuckoo, and several of Borneo's nine pitta species. Canopy walkways allow eye level birding in Sepilok and Danum Valley.
before.whaleWatching: Irrawaddy dolphins are regularly seen on boat cruises from Santubong near Kuching, mostly from April to November, and are harder to find in the wet season. Indo-Pacific finless porpoises live along the Sarawak coast all year, but no trips are built around them.
before.mountaineering: Mount Kinabalu (4,095m) is a guided trek with a short rope section near the summit rather than technical climbing, though the Mountain Torq via ferrata on its slopes adds a genuine vertical route. Sabah Parks caps climbers at 163 a day, a guide is mandatory, and bookings fill months ahead; the peak season is March to September.
before.beachesSwimming: Malaysian Borneo's east coast (Sabah) gets the real seasonal disruption — the northeast monsoon (Nov-Feb, peak Dec-Jan) brings rough seas and real storm risk; the rest of the year is calm and warm.
before.wildlifeViewing: Wild orangutans, Bornean pygmy elephants, and proboscis monkeys are the primary draws along the Kinabatangan River and in Danum Valley's rainforest, best reached via river cruise. Night walks reveal nocturnal species like slow lorises and tarsiers, and green and hawksbill turtles are reliably seen around Sipadan and Mabul.

before.birding: High-altitude specialists define birding in this trans-Himalayan desert, led by the vulnerable Black-necked Crane, which breeds at high-elevation lakes like Tso Moriri. Ibisbills are regularly seen foraging in the shingle beds of the Indus River, while Himalayan and Tibetan Snowcocks inhabit the steep slopes near high mountain passes. Golden Eagles and Bearded Vultures are commonly seen soaring above the barren valleys.
before.mountaineering: A gateway to non-technical and lightly technical trekking peaks — Kang Yatse II (6,250m) is a crampons-and-axe walk-up — with 7,000m Nun Kun via Kargil for real expeditions. Peaks above 6,000m need Indian Mountaineering Foundation clearance, and Stok Kangri, the region’s best-known peak, is reported closed to expeditions since a December 2023 order.
before.wildlifeViewing: Ladakh's marquee draw is the snow leopard, an elusive apex predator that is genuinely possible to spot on dedicated winter tracking expeditions in Hemis National Park and Ulley. The rugged terrain also supports frequently seen herds of blue sheep (bharal) and Asiatic ibex. In summer, the high-altitude Changthang plateau holds roaming herds of kiang (Tibetan wild ass), rare Tibetan antelope, and Himalayan marmots.
before.wildflowerBlooms: Ladakh's apricot orchards across the Nubra and Sham valleys erupt into white-pink blossom for a couple of weeks each spring — genuinely picturesque against the high-desert backdrop, and the reason for the region's own Apricot Blossom Festival. The window is narrow and weather-dependent, typically the first half of April.

before.birding: Wintering waterfowl on the Han River, including Mandarin Ducks and Smew, offer the best birding within Seoul, while Red-crowned and White-naped Cranes winter near the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) at Cheorwon, a long day trip. Forested parks like Bukhansan and Namsan hold resident Varied Tits and Daurian Redstarts, with migrating flycatchers and buntings in spring and fall.
before.whaleWatching: Indo-Pacific finless porpoises inhabit the Yellow Sea and are occasionally spotted from ferries or the coast near Incheon, an hour from Seoul. Sightings are chance encounters, with no dedicated boat trips.
before.mountaineering: Bukhansan’s granite peaks sit inside the Seoul metro area — Insubong is a roughly 200m slab-and-crack wall where Yvon Chouinard put up routes in the 1960s, reached by shared taxi from Ui Station and free to enter — a rare big-city trad scene. Spring and autumn are the climbing seasons; the summer monsoon and winter cold shut it down.
before.wildlifeViewing: Korean water deer are frequently seen foraging on the forested slopes of Bukhansan National Park. Raccoon dogs are occasionally spotted during night walks near urban streams like Yangjaecheon. Winter day trips to the DMZ offer reliable sightings of marquee Red-crowned Cranes.
before.wildflowerBlooms: Seoul's cherry blossom season, centered on the Yeouido Spring Flower Festival along the Han River, is a real, comparably-scaled event to Japan's — millions of visitors, a dedicated festival — but the window is short and specific: roughly the first half of April, occasionally slipping a few days earlier or later with the spring weather.

before.birding: Mute Swans and Tufted Ducks gather along the Vltava River, offering easy viewing in the city center. Large urban parks like Stromovka hold common Central European woodland species including Black Woodpeckers and Eurasian Nuthatches.
before.mountaineering: Sandstone tower climbing with its own strict tradition — Adršpach-Teplice’s towers, Prachov, and Saxon Switzerland across the border — climbed without chalk, cams, or nuts, using only ring bolts and knotted slings. It’s world-class for the tradition rather than convenience: the towers are roughly 90–150km from Prague, and wet sandstone is off-limits.
before.wildlifeViewing: Eurasian red squirrels are frequently seen in large urban green spaces like Stromovka and Petřín Hill. Along the Vltava River, introduced nutria (coypu) are common year-round, while European hares and roe deer are occasionally spotted at dawn in the Divoká Šárka reserve.

before.diving: A specialist cold-water destination strictly for experienced drysuit divers. Underwater sights include submerged ice formations, kelp forests, sea angels, and small Arctic marine life, usually accessed via summer expedition cruises.
before.birding: The high Arctic pack ice offers excellent chances to find the elusive Ivory Gull, a highly sought-after marquee species often spotted scavenging on the ice. Summer expedition cruises visit towering basalt cliffs like Alkefjellet, which hold hundreds of thousands of breeding Brünnich's Guillemots and Black-legged Kittiwakes. Inland, the endemic Svalbard Ptarmigan and Snow Buntings are reliably seen on the tundra.
before.auroraChasing: Svalbard sits right under the auroral oval — even a quiet night can deliver, no storm required. Late April to late August, though, the sun never sets, so there's no dark sky to see it against.
before.whaleWatching: **Minke** and **fin whales** are the whales most often seen from summer boat trips and expedition cruises out of Longyearbyen, with **humpbacks** sometimes found, **belugas** occasionally seen along the coast, and **blue whales** a prize that a dedicated charter looks for in June and July. The short viewing season runs from June to September when the sea ice retreats enough to allow ships to navigate the archipelago.
before.mountaineering: Not technical rock climbing but a serious polar ski-mountaineering destination — Newtontoppen (1,713m), the highest point, needs no climbing experience, while Perriertoppen is steeper and uses crampons. Late April and May, with the midnight sun arriving around 20 April, are the signature months; travel outside the settlements requires a polar-bear rifle.
before.wildlifeViewing: Polar bears are the anchor of Svalbard, reliably seen by scanning pack ice and shorelines from summer expedition cruises. Endemic, short-legged Svalbard reindeer and Arctic foxes are frequently seen year-round near Longyearbyen. Walruses gather at established haul-outs, and the surrounding waters are home to belugas and migratory whales. Viewing requires ice-strengthened ships in summer or guided snowmobiles in winter.

before.birding: Three flamingo species, the Andean, Chilean and the localized James's, congregate in the thousands at high-altitude mineral lakes like Laguna Colorada. Beyond the flamingos, Lesser Rheas stride across the surrounding altiplano, and Andean Avocets and Andean Geese feed at the lagoons, typically seen during multi-day 4x4 tours.
before.hotSprings: Termas de Polques, beside Laguna Salada near the Salvador Dalí Desert geysers, is a fixed stop on the multi-day 4x4 tours that cross the Uyuni salt flats — visited regardless of season. At over 4,300m, June and July nights are the coldest of the year, sharpening the contrast against the warm water.
before.wildlifeViewing: Three flamingo species—Andean, Chilean, and the rare James's—congregate at high-altitude mineral lagoons like Laguna Colorada, serving as the region's marquee draw. Wild vicuñas frequently graze the Altiplano scrub, while Andean viscachas are reliably spotted sunning on the rocky outcrops of Isla Incahuasi. Andean foxes and Lesser Rheas are occasionally seen on 4x4 traverses.

before.safari: Beyond its famous primates, Uganda's safari circuit centers on boat cruises and savanna drives in Murchison Falls and Queen Elizabeth National Parks. **Elephants**, **buffalo**, and **hippos** are abundant along the Kazinga Channel and the Victoria Nile, while **lions** are regularly seen. The dry seasons from June to August and December to February offer the most reliable game viewing and accessible tracks.
before.birding: Uganda's 1,000-plus species reflect three biomes meeting in one country. West and Central African rainforest birds such as Great Blue Turaco, Blue-headed Bee-eater and Piping Hornbill occur near the eastern edge of their range, while the Albertine Rift adds endemics like African Green Broadbill and Rwenzori Turaco in Bwindi. Northern savanna specialties, including Abyssinian Ground-Hornbill and Northern Carmine Bee-eater, occur at Murchison Falls. Shoebills turn up on most Mabamba Swamp boat trips, and Green-breasted Pittas call in Kibale.
before.mountaineering: The Rwenzori Mountains — the “Mountains of the Moon” — offer a genuine equatorial glacier expedition to Margherita Peak (5,109m), with crampons, fixed lines, and compulsory guides and porters. It’s a week-long trek-and-climb rather than a quick objective, with two dry seasons: a longer one from June to August and a shorter one from December to February.
before.wildlifeViewing: Mountain gorillas and chimpanzees are the biggest draws, reliably found on guided treks in Bwindi Impenetrable Forest and Kibale National Park. 12 species of monkeys include endangered Ugandan Red Colobus monkeys, rare golden monkeys, striking L'Hoest's guenons, and long-legged patas monkeys in the northern grasslands. Savanna parks like Queen Elizabeth and Murchison Falls are safari hubs with frequently seen elephants, hippos, and lions.

before.diving: Madeira offers a mix of volcanic reefs, walls, caves, and wrecks in the clear Atlantic water, including the Garajau Nature Reserve with its large, friendly dusky groupers. Divers and snorkelers can expect to see groupers, moray eels, and barracudas, with rays and occasional mobulas in late summer, which also brings the best conditions.
before.birding: The critically endangered Zino's Petrel draws dedicated birders to Madeira's offshore waters on specialized pelagic trips. Inland, the ancient Laurissilva forest holds two true endemics: the Trocaz Pigeon and the Madeira Firecrest, both reliably seen on the levada trails. While the overall species count is low, Macaronesian specialties like Berthelot's Pipit and the Atlantic Canary make it a distinct destination.
before.surfing: Real, if modest, Atlantic surf exists on the island's north coast — genuinely secondary to the famous levada hiking trails.
before.whaleWatching: **Sperm whales** and **bottlenose dolphins** are reliably seen year-round in the deep waters just offshore, with boat trips leaving directly from Funchal. The volcanic island's steep drop-off means trips find resident species within a few miles of the coast, while migratory **fin** and **Bryde's whales** pass through from April to October.
before.mountaineering: Minor — about 27 catalogued crags, mostly sport routes on São Lourenço, plus bouldering near Funchal and deep-water soloing; there’s no topo guide or via ferrata, and Pico Ruivo (1,861m) is a hike, not a climb. Climbing is possible in winter, spring, and autumn, with summer better for deep-water soloing.
before.beachesSwimming: Madeira's volcanic coast has little natural sand — most real swimming here is from rocky platforms or the island's man-made sea pools, in mild (66-72°F), fairly stable Atlantic water year-round.
before.wildlifeViewing: Resident sperm whales and bottlenose dolphins are reliably spotted year-round on deep-water boat tours from Funchal. The critically endangered Mediterranean monk seal maintains a fragile, elusive population around the protected Desertas Islands, while endemic wall lizards are omnipresent.
before.wildflowerBlooms: Madeira runs its own Flower Festival each spring, and the island's volcanic soil and mild climate support a genuinely unusual concentration of endemic flora alongside it — not just an imported display.

before.birding: The endemic Inca Wren forages in the bamboo around the Machu Picchu ruins, where Green-and-white Hummingbirds and Masked Fruiteaters turn up in the surrounding forest, and Torrent Ducks work the Urubamba's rapids. The Manu Road, a long day's drive east of Cusco, drops from high Andean grassland through cloud forest toward the Amazon, with Andean Cock-of-the-rock leks and Sword-billed Hummingbirds. High passes like Abra Málaga hold Polylepis specialists, including the critically endangered Royal Cinclodes, and soaring Andean Condors.
before.hotSprings: Three real, separate hot springs sit along Peru's most popular routes: Aguas Calientes at the base of Machu Picchu, Cocalmayo on the Sacred Valley/Salkantay trek route, and La Calera in Colca Canyon, fed by the Cotallaulli volcano. All three are more of a stopover than a reason to plan a trip around on their own.
before.mountaineering: Real technical mountaineering exists here, centered on Ausangate (6,384m) — genuine glacier travel and a roped ice wall, not a walk-up. But it’s a secondary layer on Cusco’s dominant identity as a trekking hub, not Peru’s real climbing center — that’s Huaraz, a different region entirely. The dry season (May–September) is best for both.
before.beachesSwimming: The Sacred Valley and Cusco are high-altitude and inland — swimming isn't a real feature of this destination at all; any water time is incidental, not a reason to visit.
before.wildlifeViewing: Andean Condors are frequently seen soaring over high passes and deep gorges like the Apurímac Canyon. In the high-altitude puna, wild vicuñas are occasionally spotted on remote treks like Ausangate, alongside ubiquitous domesticated llama and alpaca herds. Around Machu Picchu's rocky ruins, wild viscachas are common, and elusive Andean bears are occasionally spotted in the surrounding cloud forest.

surfing.reason: High Andes; the Pacific surf coast is a long way off.

before.diving: Accessible as a day trip to the Red Sea at Aqaba, about an hour from Wadi Rum and two hours from Petra, this area offers excellent shore and house-reef diving with no boat needed, plus the Cedar Pride wreck at 80-90 ft just off the beach. Visitors explore vibrant coral reef scenery and its fish, with main sites reaching depths up to 130 ft.
before.birding: The pale pink Sinai Rosefinch and the glossy Tristram's Starling are frequently seen among the sandstone gorges of Petra. Wadi Rum holds desert specialists like Sand Partridge and White-crowned Wheatear, best found on early morning walks. During spring and autumn, the region becomes a major flyway bottleneck, with thousands of migrating raptors passing overhead.
before.hotSprings: Ma'in Hot Springs, between Madaba and the Dead Sea, is a waterfall cascading into natural thermal pools that Herod the Great reportedly used for his health. This is a heat-avoidance story, not a cold-contrast one — summer temperatures here top 104°F, making the already-warm springs genuinely uncomfortable.
before.mountaineering: Wadi Rum, about 320km south of Amman and a separate trip from Petra, offers sandstone multi-pitch trad routes of 400–800m plus some bolted climbing, with a strong Bedouin adventure feel; a guide is needed for most areas. The season is October to April, with the shoulder months hot enough that only shaded routes work; June to August is not climbable.
before.beachesSwimming: The Dead Sea is a genuinely unique floating experience, not conventional swimming — the Gulf of Aqaba nearby offers real, warm Red Sea swimming, cooler in the depths of winter.
before.wildlifeViewing: Rock hyraxes are frequently seen sunning among the ancient sandstone ruins of Petra. In the broader desert of Wadi Rum, Nubian ibex and red foxes are genuinely elusive, requiring dedicated dawn or dusk tracking. Blue Sinai agama lizards are common on warm rocks.

before: San Cristóbal sits at 2,200m and stays genuinely cool — even cold at night — a sharp contrast to Palenque's hot, humid jungle. Dry season (Nov–Apr) is best for touring both; rainy season (May–Oct) makes Sumidero Canyon and the waterfalls more dramatic but the roads slower.

surfing.reason: Desert interior, far from any coast.

whaleWatching.reason: Central Australia, 1,500 km from the sea.

before.birding: Three species of flamingos (Andean, Chilean, and the rare James's) are reliably seen feeding together in the shallow, high-altitude salt lakes of Reserva Nacional Los Flamencos. Beyond the salt flats, the altiplano lagoons support Giant Coots, Andean Geese, Andean Avocets, and Puna Plovers. Lesser Rheas are occasionally spotted near Laguna Miscanti.
before.hotSprings: Termas de Puritama's eight geothermal pools sit in a canyon outside San Pedro de Atacama, considered sacred for centuries by the Atacameño people before opening to visitors. The desert's cold, clear nights — especially June and July — make for the sharpest hot-water contrast.
before.mountaineering: The volcanoes above San Pedro offer real altitude mountaineering — Licancabur (5,916m) is climbed from the Bolivian side because the Chilean slope is mined, as a two-day guided trip, while access to Láscar depends on volcanic alert levels. Ojos del Salado (6,893m), the world’s highest volcano, is a separate expedition staged from Copiapó, about 260km south, with its season running November to March.
before.wildlifeViewing: Vicuñas and guanacos are reliably seen grazing across the high-altitude salt flats and altiplano scrub, while nearby lagoons hold three flamingo species — Andean, Chilean, and the rare James's Flamingo. Southern viscachas are frequently spotted sunning on boulders.
before.wildflowerBlooms: In most years the Atacama — the driest desert on Earth — stays exactly that: bone dry, no flowers. Roughly once every 5 to 7 years, and increasingly unpredictable as rainfall patterns shift, an unusually wet winter triggers the Desierto Florido: dormant seeds burst into bloom across otherwise barren ground, carpeting stretches of desert in pink, purple, and yellow for a few weeks. There's no way to predict a specific year in advance — a bloom is typically only confirmed once it's already underway.

before.diving: The Mediterranean coast of Provence, particularly the Calanques National Park near Marseille, offers steep limestone drop-offs, caves, and historic shipwrecks. Divers can spot groupers, moray eels, and octopus in clear blue water, while snorkelers explore the sheltered rocky coves.
before.birding: Greater Flamingos are the iconic draw of the Camargue wetlands, reliably seen year-round in Europe's largest river delta. Beyond the marshes, the stony steppe of La Crau holds Pin-tailed Sandgrouse and Little Bustards, while the limestone cliffs of the Alpilles support Bonelli's Eagles and Eurasian Eagle-Owls. Spring and autumn migrations bring massive numbers of waders and colorful summer visitors like European Bee-eaters.
before.surfing: Not really a surf destination — this is a lavender-and-hill-towns region, and any real coastline is well outside its scope.
before.windSports: The Camargue coast, especially Beauduc and the beaches near Les Saintes-Maries-de-la-Mer, is one of France's best-known kitesurfing regions — driven by the Mistral, a powerful wind funneled down the Rhône valley. The Mistral is strongest and most frequent November through April, but it can blow at any time of year, including a lighter autumn presence.
before.whaleWatching: **Fin whales** and **striped dolphins** are the main draws, with full-day naturalist-led cruises from Sanary-sur-Mer running from April to November into the Pelagos Sanctuary. Spring and autumn suit fin whales and summer evenings suit dolphins, but trips travel far offshore and sightings are never certain.
before.mountaineering: Provence’s climbing is in the Verdon Gorge — over 1,500 routes, with multi-pitch limestone lines of 100–350m, about an hour and three-quarters from Aix — plus the sea cliffs of the Calanques near Marseille and the 500-route crag at Buoux. Spring and autumn are best; summer is too hot and the Calanques close for fire risk, and winter is too cold for the gorge.
before.beachesSwimming: Provence's Mediterranean coast (the Camargue and coastal towns) gives this a real, if secondary, Mediterranean swim option — cold in winter, genuinely warm by midsummer.
before.wildlifeViewing: Greater Flamingos are reliably seen year-round in the Camargue wetlands, alongside wild boar and introduced coypu. Off the coast of Marseille and Cassis, the Pelagos Sanctuary hosts summer populations of fin and sperm whales, accessible via certified boat tours. Inland scrublands support elusive Hermann’s tortoises and frequently spotted ocellated lizards.
before.wildflowerBlooms: Valensole's lavender fields are the reason people plan trips to Provence specifically for this — but the window is short and cut for oil potency, not visual peak, so it can close early in a hot year. The Valensole lavender festival is fixed to the third Sunday of July, but by then the fields are sometimes already harvested; the most reliable peak color runs late June into the first ten days of July.

For whales passing through the Lombok Strait I found only stranding reports (three large whales on Bali in April 2023), no live sightings from tours, so that clause is unsupported. Suggested text change (not applied): Suggest dropping "Whales occasionally pass through the Lombok Strait". Mention Bondalem as a quieter alternative if you want.

Corrected. A Kochi survey (October 2018 to September 2019) recorded four dolphin species: Indo-Pacific humpback, spinner, Indo-Pacific bottlenose and long-beaked common dolphins, mostly within 50 metres depth, fewer in the monsoon. Humpback dolphins also use the Vembanad backwaters. I found no finless porpoise record for Kerala (the nearest is from Mangalore, in Karnataka), so the overview and cell are unsupported there. Suggested text change (not applied): Removes finless porpoises and adds spinner and bottlenose dolphins; sightings are fewer in the monsoon.

The highest leopard population density recorded anywhere on Earth (25-30 per 100 km²) — with no lions or tigers to compete with, Yala's leopards are unusually large, bold, and habituated to safari vehicles. Best: Dry season, Feb–Jun, for the best sightings (Block 1 especially). Same country as the catalog's existing srilanka entry (already authored for "The Gathering" elephants) — a completely different claim: leopards, not elephants, and a different park. (Established. From the Catalog Wishlist.)

Zambia's largest park at 22,400 km² — one of the largest in Africa — rapidly recovering under African Parks management, with a genuine diversity of habitats (miombo woodland, floodplains, wetlands) supporting species South Luangwa doesn't, including cheetah and blue wildebeest. Best: Dry season, Jun–Oct, for the best access and viewing. Same country as the catalog's existing zambia entry (South Luangwa) — a much larger, ecologically distinct park in central-western Zambia, not a restatement of the Luangwa Valley's river-corridor story. (Real, specialist-known. From the Catalog Wishlist.)

A 40km Lake Erie sand spit; home to the longest continuously running bird observatory in the Americas (since 1960). Best: Spring Mar–May; fall Sep–Nov (raptors, sandhill cranes). Distinct from Point Pelee despite the same lake — different institutional identity, long-term banding research. (Real, specialist-known. From the Catalog Wishlist.)

Cape Verde Shearwater (breeds nowhere else) and the Raso Lark, confined to a single 7km² islet. Best: Shearwaters Feb–Oct. A Western Palearctic seabird specialty destination for listers chasing the Raso Lark and Fea's Petrel. (Real, specialist-known. From the Catalog Wishlist.) ↳ Also on the diving list (same name).

Humpback whales travel about 8,500 km from Antarctica to breed and calve in the warm Chocó waters (Utría National Park is a key refuge). Best: Jul–Nov, peak Aug–Sep. A different coast from Colombia's Caribbean side, a growing ecotourism draw on a smaller scale than Australia or Hawaii. (Real, specialist-known. From the Catalog Wishlist.)

A major North Pacific humpback whale breeding ground about 1,000 km south of Tokyo; Chichijima's waters are key habitat. Best: Late Nov–May, peak Feb–Apr. Reachable only by a roughly 24-hour ferry, which keeps volumes modest. (Established. From the Catalog Wishlist.)
